query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under tribological stress in corrosive environments, mechanical deformation of high-entropy alloys induces a dynamic near-surface nanocrystalline layer that rapidly oxidizes to form a protective passivation film, which in turn suppresses both wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with relatively coarse grains and minimal pre-existing oxide films.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to sliding wear in a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., aqueous solution with dissolved oxygen) compared to tests in an inert environment.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under similar mechanical loads and sliding speeds, with one set in an oxidizing (corrosive) medium and another in an inert medium, ensuring controlled pH, oxygen availability, and temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer through dynamic amorphization under mechanical stress, which then promotes rapid and uniform oxide passivation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical deformation during wear refines the grain structure and induces amorphization near the surface. The resulting nanocrystalline structure has a high density of reactive sites that facilitates rapid oxidation, forming a protective oxide film. This dual effect minimizes further mechanical wearing and limits aggressive metal dissolution by stabilizing the surface electrochemically.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline condition (e.g., similar alloy tested in an inert environment or one lacking dynamic nanocrystallization), the coupled tribo-corrosion degradation (total material loss) will be reduced, as both the wear component and the corrosion component are attenuated by the rapid formation of a protective passivated layer.
generation.baseline: The typical wear and corrosion behavior observed in HEAs without significant dynamic nanocrystalline layer formation (or in inert environments where oxidation is suppressed).
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to hold when the environment provides sufficient oxygen and electrochemical potential for oxidation; it may fail or be less effective in conditions that are either highly reducing or where the oxidation kinetics are too slow due to low temperature or inadequate oxidant concentration.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of improvement in wear and corrosion resistance as well as the precise interplay between wear debris removal and oxide reformation rates remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel tribo-corrosion experiments on the high-entropy alloy sample. One set is tested in an oxidizing, corrosive environment (e.g., an aqueous acidic solution with adequate dissolved oxygen) while the other is carried out in an inert environment (e.g., argon-saturated solution). Characterize the near-surface region for nanocrystallinity and oxide formation using TEM and XPS. Simultaneously measure wear rates via profilometry and corrosion rates via electrochemical techniques.
measurements: Wear volume or wear rate (via profilometry or weight loss)
Electrochemical corrosion current density and potential measurements
Surface oxide film thickness and uniformity (via TEM/XPS)
Grain size distribution in the wear track (via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under the oxidizing condition the alloy does not develop a distinct ultra-nanocrystalline and passivated surface layer (as compared to the inert environment) and if the measured wear and corrosion rates are not significantly reduced relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
